title: Chapter 1: Forty-One Over the Reedbed
blurb: The Circuit Loft's spare hand counts forty-one birds over a failing fen, and the official counter writes down forty.

blocks.text: At ten past four the light over Hobsmere Reedbed went the colour of new copper, and the flock poured itself thin and thick against the cloud. I had crated those forty Sedgeway birds myself after Friday's draw, lifting each one, feeling its heart go quick under my thumb, counting it in. Now I raised my loft glass and counted them again, because counting is my work.
The count came to forty-one.
I counted again, slowly, the way I was taught, from the leading edge back through the body of the flock to the trailing wisp, because a loft hand does not get a count wrong. Forty-one.

The Sedgeway flock had been drawn at noon on the Friday, in the yard of the Circuit Loft at Wenlode, with the public at the rail and the message pigeons muttering above the gate. Hobsmere Cutters against Gadwell Drove, at Hobsmere: the clerk turned the drum and drew the lot, and it was Sedgeway. I was glad. The Sedgeway birds are the gentlest of the six league flocks, and I knew them best.

I am the Loft's spare hand. I was the spare child in my aunt's house before that, and I think I have always known how to stand at the edge of a room. I feed when someone is ill and go with the crates to the fixtures nobody else wants, and in three winters I had never minded, because the birds did not care whose hand it was.

That afternoon I lifted the Sedgeway starlings from their flight one at a time. A starling in the hand is lighter than you expect, all feather and want, and its feet close round your finger as if your finger were a branch it had chosen. I looked at each ring, the Loft's plain alloy band, and spoke to each bird, and put it into the crate. I counted forty, and I closed the lid.
We travelled through the night along the drove roads, the dykes lying black on either side and once a barn owl going over, pale as paper in the headlamps, and by first light we were at Hobsmere.

Hobsmere is a reed-cutters' village at the edge of its own mere, and the mere was the first thing I saw: a long sheet of pewter water under a low sky, a skin of ice along the margin, a raft of tufted duck far out, and a heron working the shallows by the causeway as if nothing in the world were waiting on it. The Reedbed lay along the south-west shore, two hundred paces of reed-poles and flat water, with a thatched Roost at either end.

The causeway was too soft at the Reedbed end for the van, so the driver left it on the hard road across the water, and Wilfred Cobbing, the Hobsmere chairman, brought my crate over on his eel-cart. I walked beside it with one hand on the lid, feeling the birds shift and settle under it.
Hobsmere were bottom of the Marsh Circuit. Everyone at the rail said so in the low, careful voices people use at a bedside. They needed to win.

I watched the Ringing from the reed-line, beside my crate, because a loft hand stays with her birds. Hamish Toller, the Hobsmere Wing, closed a copper ring on the wrist of each of his crew and on his own last, and then put the withy from his hand onto the wrist of his tether, a slight young man who held his arm out stiffly as though he were afraid of creasing it. The counters drew the ends by lot and entered them on the team sheet. The lot gave Gadwell Drove the north-east Roost to attack. A groan went along the rail, and someone said, 'Northing'll have them,' and someone else told him to hush.
One of the Hobsmere Tackers came over to the crate while his Wing was busy. He had very good hair and he knew it.
'You're the bird girl,' he said. 'Watch my runs, will you, Crate? Rhys Dorne. I'm the handsome one. Remember the name, the papers always get it wrong.'
'I'll watch them,' I said. 'I watch everything under the flock.'
He looked at me a moment, as if he could not tell whether I was laughing at him. I was not. Then he grinned and went back to his place.

The tether came after him, more slowly. 'W-would you mind, miss,' he said, 'keeping the crate clear of the reed-line after the Loose? Only it sits in the run. I'm Lucas. Lucas Mbeki. I'm sorry to ask.'
'It'll be clear,' I said. 'I'll carry it back myself.'

A woman in drainage boots shouted across the field at both of them. 'You're going to stand there chatting till the light goes, are you? No? Then get in your places.' That was Joan Pettifer, one of the Hobsmere Callers. She did not look at me at all.
At twenty to four, with the wind light from the south-west and the east already thinning to the grey of a wood pigeon's wing, I knelt in the wet at the centre of the Reedbed and opened the crate.

The Loose is the part of the work I love most. For a breath the birds sit in the dark of the crate and consider the opened sky. Then all of them go together, as if they had been a single bird all along and only now remembered it, with a sound like a sheet shaken out over a bed, and the low light ran over their backs like water over stones.
Within the minute the shades rose.

I have seen shades all my life, and I do not talk about them. When I was small I said too many true things, and people looked at me afterwards in a way I did not want again, so I kept the shapes to myself: the bird-shapes that fly above the runners at a match, each one straight over the person whose copper it answers. Most people at the rail see forty birds and twelve players. I see twelve more shapes in the air, and through my loft glass I could read the copper on their legs, CCIII and 26 over Rhys Dorne as he ran, CCIII and 22 over Hamish.

Hamish herded, the way most Wings fly. His shades went out along the edge of the flock, each one leaning on the birds nearest it, and the flock answered him the way long grass answers a hand drawn over it, bending a little and coming back. He was trying to ease them west, away from his own Roost.

The Gadwell Drove Wing was a tall woman in a drover's coat, and she hardly tried to steer at all. Each time Hamish lifted or lowered his ceiling, she set hers where his was, a breath behind him, and her shades slid in among his, among the same birds, leaning the other way. For the breath it took hers to settle, his had the birds to themselves; then hers came level, and the birds that had begun to bend came back, hearing two voices saying opposite things and believing neither. It was like watching two people pull at either end of a wet sheet. The flock went where the wind and the failing light and its own slow lean had always meant it to go, which was north-east, a little at a time, towards the Roost Hobsmere were defending.
At four o'clock the counters called the Breath, and both Wings dropped every shade for a full minute, and the air over the Reedbed held only birds. Then the shades came back.
At ten past four the counters declared roost-light.

The four counters spread themselves along the reed-line to count the flock, and the nearest, a small woman in a counter's grey with a pencil behind her ear, would call the counted flock for the sheet. Her name was Dorcas Ely; I had read it at the foot of many sheets. I counted with them, because the birds were mine until I handed them back at Wenlode.

That was when I found it, the count I began with. It flew at the north-east edge of the flock, where the body thinned to a trailing wisp against the cloud, flying exactly as a starling flies and keeping its place among its neighbours as they kept theirs around it. It was over no runner. I looked down to be sure, and there was only reed and water and a moorhen going in under the bank. It was not one of the twelve. It was a forty-first bird.

I put the glass on it. The light was going, but it was good copper light still, and the Loft's glass is a good one, and I hold it steady from long practice. The bird had a ring on its leg, and it was not the Loft's alloy. It was copper, dark with age, like the copper on the shades, and the stamp on it was a single upright stroke, the numeral I, and after it a number worn so smooth I could not read it at all.
Season I was two hundred years ago.
Beside me Dorcas Ely touched her pencil to her tongue. 'Counted flock,' she said to the counter on her left, 'forty.'
'Forty-one,' I said.
I did not say it to make trouble. I said it because it was true, and I have never in my life been able to leave a wrong count standing.
Dorcas Ely's shoulders flinched as if something cold had touched her neck. She did not look up. She wrote on the sheet, and I was close enough to see what she wrote. It was forty.
'Forty, miss,' she said, to the sheet. Then again, quieter, as if once had not been enough: 'Forty, miss.'

I lowered the glass. Behind me someone had stopped moving. I turned, and it was Joan Pettifer, at the edge of the reed-line with her hands still raised from signalling, looking straight at me. Her face had gone very still. She looked at me the way a dyke-reeve looks at a bank she had thought sound when the water first comes through it. Then Hamish's hand went up out on the field, and she turned back to her work.

The Gloaming is the last of the light, when the flock begins to want its roost, and every Wing knows that what a flock wants then is what a flock will do. The Gadwell Drove Tackers ran down to the north-east Roost and planted their two wooden starlings on their poles beside its mouth, low, below head height, and the real birds, coming down out of the cold, saw birds already settled there.

Hamish tried to hold them off. He kept his shades up when he should have rested them, chasing the head of the flock along the reed-line, and every time he lifted, the woman in the drover's coat followed him up. He took his second Breath at twenty-one minutes past four and went straight back in after, his face white as fen-mist, his lips moving. Joan was signing to Mercy Ledbetter across the field and swearing between the signs. 'Silt. Silt and sumps. Come on, Hamish. Back-flowing, silted-up, come on.'

The flock leaned north-east, as flocks do, and the dark came in from the east over the mere like water filling a lock, and the birds went down into the Roost in long grey ribbons, a few and then many, the way water finds the lowest place.
At half past four it was full dark. The counters' whistles went, and the shades went out like lamps. I looked for the forty-first bird and it was gone. I had not seen it go.

The counters counted both Roosts by lantern. Twenty-four Sedgeway birds in the north-east Roost, more than half the counted flock of forty: a partial settle to Gadwell Drove, two points to nothing. The rest were in the far Roost, too few to score, or still calling in the dark, and I went along the reed-line with my recall whistle and brought them back to me one by one.
Joan stood in the lantern light with the team sheet crushed in her fist and said it to all of them, plainly, as if saying it plainly might make it smaller.

'Bottom. Ten points. Tarrow Dyke are on fifteen, so that's five from safe, with five to play. Pashley Carr on thirteen. And if we lose again, what then? Then we have to win every single match that's left and have Tarrow and Pashley Carr both fall over in the silt. That's what then.' She turned to Hamish. 'Forty-eight minutes you were up, weren't you? I heard the counters. Forty-eight.'
'Thirty-eight to walk off,' Hamish said. His voice was thin and far away. 'Lucas.'
Lucas came to him with the withy on his wrist and took his hand, and they turned together along the bank of the mere.

I took the crate back across the causeway on Wilfred Cobbing's eel-cart. The driver had lit the van's lamps on the far road, and I sat on the tailboard with the crate beside me and my hand on its lid, and waited for the counters' sheet, which a loft hand carries home with her birds.

From there I could see the Reedbed across the water. The mere is narrow at that neck, a long stone's throw and no more, and by Joan's lantern I could see the Hobsmere crew on the bank, and Hamish and Lucas walking slowly along the margin, hand in hand, Lucas talking all the while. Everyone on the Levels knows what a walk-down is. A Wing who has called too long has her sense of direction bent toward the flock she called, and she walks toward it, and her tether holds her hand and talks her down, a minute for every minute she owes. What I had not thought about, until I sat there with my hand on the lid, was where the flock was.
It was beside me. Forty birds in a crate on the tailboard of a van on the Wenlode road, and between them and Hamish Toller lay Hobsmere Mere.
He kept turning his head to look across the water, toward me. Each time, Lucas said something, and he turned back.
Then Lucas stopped.

He stopped walking and stood quite still on the bank, and he was not looking at Hamish. He was looking out over the mere, the same way Hamish was looking, toward me and the crate, with his face lifted as if he were listening to something a long way off. I saw his hand open. I saw it as plainly as I have ever seen anything, the fingers coming apart one by one in the lantern light, the withy pale on his wrist.
Hamish walked into the water.

I remember the mere. I remember that the ice at the margin was thin and grey and broke under him with a sound like a plate set down on a stone floor, and that the water beyond it was black and very still, holding the last of the light from the west in one long bar the colour of a pigeon's throat, and that the reeds on the near bank stood up out of it in their thousands, pale and dry and rattling a little in the south-west wind, and that a coot somewhere out on the dark called once and then did not call again, and that the tufted duck I had watched in the morning were gone, and that the water came up to his knees and then to his waist and he did not slow and did not look down, he walked as if the mere were a field and the crate beside me were a door left open, and I stood up on the tailboard and could not think of one single thing I could do that would reach across that water, and so I held on to the crate and watched the line he was walking, which was straight, which was perfectly straight, which ran from the lantern on the bank to my hand.
Joan went to the edge. She went to the very edge, where the ice was broken, and put both her arms out over the water as far as they would reach, and shouted his name, and she did not go in.

Rhys Dorne went in. He went past her in a long, flat dive that set the lantern light shaking across the whole mere, and Abel Bunyard went in after him, and between them they reached Hamish with the water at his chest and took him under the arms and dragged him back, though he fought them, though his face stayed turned to me the whole way. They brought him up onto the bank and held him down in the reeds, and Lucas knelt and took his hand again, and his voice came to me over the water, high and broken, beginning the walk-down again from the start.
Hamish was alive. I saw his chest heave. I saw Rhys sit back in the reeds with his good hair flat to his skull and put his face in his hands.

Dorcas Ely came across the causeway on her bicycle a little after, with the counters' sheet in an envelope. She gave it to me without getting off, and without looking at me, and rode away into the dark.
All the way to Wenlode I turned it over and could not make sense of it. Lucas had been holding on, and then he had looked out over the water and let go, as though someone had called him by name.

It was past midnight when we reached the Circuit Loft. I carried the crate into the Sedgeway flight and lifted the birds out under the lamp one at a time, as I had put them in, each one warm and cross and alive, each wearing the Loft's plain alloy ring. I settled each on its perch with my own hands, and the count was forty, as it had been on Friday, as it should be.
Then I opened the envelope. In a small neat hand: Counted flock: 40. Signed, D. Ely.

I sat on the feed bin a long while in the warm, dusty dark, with the birds breathing round me, and in memory I lifted the loft glass again and looked at the copper on that leg. The oldest Wing now flying was born a hundred and fifty years after that ring was closed.
I had crated forty birds and counted forty-one over the Reedbed, and the forty-first wore a ring stamped two hundred years ago. The counter had seen it too, and she had written it down as nothing.
